sounds.intro: Finnish is written in the Latin alphabet and is spelled exactly as it sounds. It is not related to Swedish or Russian. There are no genders and no articles. Words are long because endings pile up. The stress is always on the first syllable.
rows: say "ur" with rounded lips, like "ur" in "fur"
say "ee" with rounded lips, like German "ü"
aa / ee / ii / oo / uu / yy
a double vowel is held long
a double consonant is held long, with a pause before it
rolled, as in Spanish or Italian
notes: Double letters change the meaning. "Tuli" is fire, "tuuli" is wind, "tulli" is customs.
Vowel harmony: a word uses either back vowels (a, o, u) or front vowels (ä, ö, y) in its endings, never both. Talossa (in the house), kylässä (in the village).

grammar.title: Pronouns
text: Finnish has no he / she difference: "hän" means both. In speech people often use "se" (it) for a person and "me" or "mä" for I. "Sinä" is you (informal) and "te" is you (formal or plural).

grammar.title: Singular and plural
text: Add -t to the noun for the plain plural: kirja, kirjat. After a number, the noun stays singular and takes the "-a / -ä" ending: kaksi kirjaa (two books).

grammar.title: To be: olla
text: Learn the six forms: olen, olet, on, olemme, olette, ovat. In the third person, "on" is used for both singular and plural in speech.

grammar.title: Having: minulla on
text: Finnish has no verb "to have". It says "at me is": minulla on (I have), sinulla on (you have), hänellä on (he has). The thing owned is the subject.

grammar.title: Present tense
text: Take the infinitive, drop the ending, and add the person ending. Puhua (to speak): puhun, puhut, puhuu, puhumme, puhutte, puhuvat.

grammar.title: Basic sentences
text: The usual order is who, verb, what. Finnish has no articles, so there is no "the" or "a".

grammar.title: Negation
text: Finnish has a negative verb, "ei", which changes with the person: en, et, ei, emme, ette, eivät. The main verb stays in its short form after it.
ex: I do not have a car
he does not work on Sundays

grammar.title: Asking questions
text: Add -ko or -kö to the first word and move it to the front: Puhutko? (Do you speak?). Or use a question word.

grammar.title: Question words
text: Question words go at the start of the sentence.

grammar.title: Possessives and liking
text: Add an ending to the noun: -ni (my), -si (your), -nsa / -Vn (his, her), -mme (our), -nne (your, plural), -nsa (their). Often "minun" or "sinun" is added: minun kirjani.

grammar.title: Formal vs informal
text: sinä (informal): friends, family, children, and most people today. te (formal): older strangers, some work situations. In Finland people use "sinä" almost everywhere, even with teachers.

grammar.title: Past and future (simple)
text: Past: usually add -i- to the stem: puhun, puhuin (I spoke). Future: Finnish has no future tense. Use the present with a time word: menen huomenna (I go tomorrow).

grammar.title: Commands
text: Informal: the stem alone (tule!). Formal or plural: add -kaa / -kää (tulkaa!). To forbid, use "älä": älä tule!

grammar.title: Can, must, want
text: Osata / voida (can): osaan, voin + infinitive. Täytyy / pitää (must): minun täytyy mennä. Haluta (want): haluan mennä.
ex: I do not want to eat

grammar.title: In, on, at
text: Finnish uses endings, not words in front. Inside: -ssa / -ssä (in), -sta / -stä (out of), -han / -hin (into). Outside: -lla / -llä (on, at), -lta / -ltä (from), -lle (onto, to).
ex: the book is on the table
the cat is under the table
the shop is next to the bank
the park is near the station
the key is in the bag

grammar.title: Comparing things
text: Add -mpi for "more": iso, isompi. "Than" is "kuin". For "the most", add -in: isoin.
